slides.headline: How does a bear live on termites?
slides.sub: Missing front teeth, sealable nostrils, and feeding noises heard up to 185 m away

slides.headline: Rip it open, then shut the nose
slides.body: Long, curved claws tear into the termite nest. The bear can close its nostrils completely, so it doesn't inhale the dust it blows away.
slides.source: Animal Diversity Web; Smithsonian's National Zoo

slides.headline: A gap where the front teeth should be
slides.body: Adult sloth bears are missing their top two front teeth (incisors). Through the gap, they suck termites and other insects up with ease.

slides.label: how far its feeding puffs and belches can be heard
slides.body: Outside the fruiting season, insects make up about 95% of a sloth bear's diet.
slides.source: Animal Diversity Web; Smithsonian's National Zoo

slides.headline: Cubs ride on mum's back
slides.body: A cub clings to the shaggy 'saddle' of fur on its mother's back until it is 6 to 9 months old.

slides.headline: Vulnerable, and declining
slides.body: IUCN lists the sloth bear as Vulnerable (assessed 2016, published 2020) and decreasing. Habitat loss and conflict with people are the main threats.

caption:
How does a bear live on termites? The sloth bear (Melursus ursinus) is missing its top two front teeth, can seal its nostrils shut, and feeds so noisily it can be heard up to 185 m away.

It rips a termite mound open with its claws, blows the loose soil away with its nose closed, then sucks the insects in through the gap in its teeth. There is no reliable range-wide count of sloth bears; IUCN lists the species as Vulnerable with a decreasing trend across India, Sri Lanka and Nepal.
